answer: Under Section 29 of DPDP Act 2023, any person aggrieved by an order of the Data Protection Board may prefer an appeal to the Telecom Disputes Settlement and Appellate Tribunal (TDSAT) within 60 days.
source_title: India Code - Digital Repository of All Central and State Acts

question: What constitutes Domestic Violence under Section 3 of the DV Act, 2005?
answer: Section 3 defines domestic violence broadly to include physical abuse, sexual abuse, verbal and emotional abuse (insults, humiliation), and economic abuse (deprivation of financial resources, maintenance, or household necessities) by an adult male in a domestic relationship.
act_name: Protection of Women from Domestic Violence Act, 2005
source_title: India Code - Digital Repository of All Central and State Acts

question: What is the Right to Reside in a Shared Household under Section 17 of the DV Act?
answer: Section 17 guarantees every woman in a domestic relationship the statutory right to reside in the shared household, regardless of whether she has any title or ownership right. She cannot be evicted or excluded save in accordance with procedure established by law.
act_name: Protection of Women from Domestic Violence Act, 2005
source_title: Supreme Court of India Official Portal

question: What reliefs can a Magistrate grant under the Domestic Violence Act?
answer: Under Sections 18 to 22, the Magistrate can grant: Protection Orders (prohibiting violence/communication), Residence Orders (restraining eviction), Monetary Relief (maintenance/medical expenses), Custody Orders (temporary child custody), and Compensation Orders for damages.
act_name: Protection of Women from Domestic Violence Act, 2005
source_title: India Code - Digital Repository of All Central and State Acts

question: What is the role of Protection Officers under Section 9 of the DV Act?
answer: Protection Officers (appointed in every district) assist the Magistrate, prepare Domestic Incident Reports (DIR), assist the aggrieved woman in accessing free legal aid, police assistance, medical facilities, and safe shelter homes.
act_name: Protection of Women from Domestic Violence Act, 2005
source_title: India Code - Digital Repository of All Central and State Acts

question: What is the penalty for breaching a Protection Order under Section 31 of DV Act?
answer: Under Section 31 of DV Act, breach of a protection order by the respondent is a cognizable and non-bailable criminal offence punishable with imprisonment up to one year, or fine up to ₹20,000, or both.
act_name: Protection of Women from Domestic Violence Act, 2005
source_title: India Code - Digital Repository of All Central and State Acts

question: What is an Internal Complaints Committee (ICC) under Section 4 of POSH Act, 2013?
answer: Section 4 of POSH Act mandates every workplace with 10 or more employees to constitute an ICC headed by a senior woman employee, with not less than half female members and one independent external member from an NGO familiar with sexual harassment issues.
act_name: Sexual Harassment of Women at Workplace Act, 2013
source_title: India Code - Digital Repository of All Central and State Acts

question: What is the Local Complaints Committee (LCC) under Section 6 of POSH Act?
answer: Section 6 mandates the District Officer to constitute a Local Committee in every district to receive sexual harassment complaints from workplaces having fewer than 10 employees or where the complaint is against the employer himself.
act_name: Sexual Harassment of Women at Workplace Act, 2013
source_title: India Code - Digital Repository of All Central and State Acts

question: What is the timeline for filing a complaint under Section 9 of the POSH Act?
answer: Under Section 9 of POSH Act, a written complaint must be submitted to the ICC/LCC within 3 months from the date of the incident (extendable by another 3 months if sufficient cause prevented timely filing).
act_name: Sexual Harassment of Women at Workplace Act, 2013
source_title: India Code - Digital Repository of All Central and State Acts

question: What is Conciliation under Section 10 of POSH Act and can monetary settlement be made?
answer: Under Section 10, before initiating inquiry, ICC can at complainant's request take steps to settle the matter through conciliation. However, the statute strictly forbids monetary settlement as the basis of conciliation.
act_name: Sexual Harassment of Women at Workplace Act, 2013
source_title: India Code - Digital Repository of All Central and State Acts

question: What are the inquiry powers and timeline of the ICC under POSH Act?
answer: Under Section 11, the ICC exercises civil court powers to summon witnesses and examine documents. The inquiry must be completed within 90 days, and the employer must act on recommendations within 60 days (Section 13).
act_name: Sexual Harassment of Women at Workplace Act, 2013
source_title: India Code - Digital Repository of All Central and State Acts

question: What is Quid Pro Quo and Hostile Work Environment under POSH Act?
answer: Under Section 3, sexual harassment includes implied/explicit promise of preferential treatment or threat of detrimental treatment in employment (quid pro quo), or conduct creating an intimidating, hostile, or offensive work environment.
act_name: Sexual Harassment of Women at Workplace Act, 2013
source_title: India Code - Digital Repository of All Central and State Acts

question: What are the confidentiality mandates under Section 16 of the POSH Act?
answer: Section 16 prohibits publication or disclosure of the identity of the aggrieved woman, respondent, witnesses, or inquiry proceedings to the public or press, despite anything in RTI. Violations attract employer penalties under Section 17.
act_name: Sexual Harassment of Women at Workplace Act, 2013
source_title: India Code - Digital Repository of All Central and State Acts

question: What is the Maternity Leave entitlement under the Maternity Benefit (Amendment) Act, 2017?
answer: Section 5 of the Maternity Benefit Act entitles women employees to 26 weeks of fully paid maternity leave for up to two surviving children (and 12 weeks for third child onward), with up to 8 weeks taken prior to expected delivery.
source_title: India Code - Digital Repository of All Central and State Acts

question: What are the Crèche facility requirements under Section 11A of Maternity Benefit Act?
answer: Section 11A mandates that every establishment with 50 or more employees must provide a crèche facility within prescribed distance, allowing four visits a day by the mother including rest intervals.
source_title: India Code - Digital Repository of All Central and State Acts

question: Can an employer terminate or dismiss a woman during maternity leave?
answer: Under Section 12 of the Maternity Benefit Act, it is strictly unlawful for an employer to discharge, dismiss, or reduce wages of a woman during her maternity leave absence or give notice of termination expiring during such period.
source_title: India Code - Digital Repository of All Central and State Acts

question: What special protections exist for the arrest of women under Section 43 of BNSS (formerly 46(4) CrPC)?
answer: Section 43(5) of BNSS 2023 (formerly Section 46(4) CrPC) mandates that no woman shall be arrested after sunset and before sunrise, except in unavoidable circumstances with prior permission of a Judicial Magistrate, and arrests must be carried out by female police officers.
source_title: India Code - Digital Repository of All Central and State Acts

question: What is the right of a woman victim to have her statement recorded by a woman magistrate/officer?
answer: Under Section 183 of BNSS (formerly 164 CrPC), statements and confessions of women victims in sexual offences must be recorded by a woman Judicial Magistrate, and at victim's residence or place of choice.
source_title: India Code - Digital Repository of All Central and State Acts

question: What is Zero FIR and can a woman register it at any police station?
answer: Under Section 173 of BNSS 2023, an FIR can be registered at any police station regardless of territorial jurisdiction (Zero FIR). The station must register the complaint, initiate immediate inquiry, and transfer it to the jurisdictional station.
source_title: India Code - Digital Repository of All Central and State Acts

question: What is the Prohibition of Dowry under the Dowry Prohibition Act, 1961?
answer: Under Section 3 of Dowry Prohibition Act, 1961, giving, taking, or abetting the giving or taking of dowry is an offence punishable with imprisonment of not less than 5 years and fine not less than ₹15,000 or the value of the dowry.
source_title: India Code - Digital Repository of All Central and State Acts

question: What is Stridhan and does the husband or in-laws have any claim over it?
answer: Stridhan includes all gifts, jewelry, cash, and property received by a woman before, during, or after marriage. In Pratibha Rani v. Suraj Kumar (1985), the Supreme Court ruled that a woman is the absolute owner of Stridhan; refusal to return it amounts to criminal breach of trust (Section 316 BNS).
source_title: Supreme Court of India Official Portal

question: What is the Medical Termination of Pregnancy (Amendment) Act, 2021 gestation limit?
answer: Under the MTP Act, abortion is legally permitted up to 20 weeks with the opinion of one registered medical practitioner, and up to 24 weeks for special categories (rape survivors, minors, fetal abnormalities) with the opinion of two doctors.
source_title: India Code - Digital Repository of All Central and State Acts

question: What is the Prohibition of Sex Selection under the PCPNDT Act, 1994?
answer: The Pre-Conception and Pre-Natal Diagnostic Techniques Act, 1994 strictly prohibits sex selection and prenatal sex determination techniques to prevent female feticide, penalizing doctors and clinics with imprisonment up to 3 years and deregistration.
source_title: India Code - Digital Repository of All Central and State Acts

question: What is the National Commission for Women (NCW) and its complaint mechanism?
answer: Established under NCW Act, 1990, the National Commission for Women reviews constitutional and legal safeguards for women, investigates complaints of atrocities, and provides a 24/7 Women Helpline (7827170170) and online complaint portal.
source_title: NCW Official Portal

question: What is the Two-Finger Test and is it banned in rape investigations?
answer: The Supreme Court in State of Jharkhand v. Shailendra Kumar Rai (2022) strictly banned the regressive 'two-finger test', holding that conducting it violates a rape survivor's dignity and bodily integrity under Article 21, warning that practitioners will be guilty of misconduct.
source_title: Supreme Court of India Official Portal

question: Can a live-in partner seek protection and maintenance under the DV Act?
answer: In D. Velusamy v. D. Patchaiammal (2010), the Supreme Court held that women in relationships 'in the nature of marriage' (long cohabitation, pooled resources, held out as spouses) are entitled to protection and maintenance under the Domestic Violence Act.
act_name: Protection of Women from Domestic Violence Act, 2005
source_title: Supreme Court of India Official Portal

question: What is the Women in Distress Helpline number across India?
answer: Women in distress can contact the All-India Women Helpline at **1091**, the Domestic Abuse National Helpline at **181**, or the unified emergency response support system at **112** for 24/7 immediate assistance.
act_name: Ministry of Women and Child Development
source_title: WCD Official Portal

question: What is the One Stop Centre (Sakhi) Scheme for women affected by violence?
answer: The Sakhi One Stop Centre scheme established by the Central Government provides integrated support under one roof (medical aid, police assistance, psycho-social counseling, legal aid, and temporary shelter) to women affected by violence.
act_name: Ministry of Women and Child Development
source_title: WCD Official Portal

question: What are the property rights of tribal women under Hindu Succession Act?
answer: Section 2(2) of HSA 1956 excludes Scheduled Tribes from the Hindu Succession Act unless the Central Government notifies. In Kamla Neti v. Special Land Acquisition Officer (2022), the Supreme Court urged the Union Government to amend the law to grant equal inheritance to tribal women.
source_title: Supreme Court of India Official Portal

question: What constitutes voyeurism and non-consensual photography under BNS Section 77?
answer: Under Section 77 of BNS 2023, capturing or publishing images of a woman engaging in a private act without consent carries imprisonment up to 3 years and fine on first conviction, and up to 7 years on repeat conviction.
source_title: India Code - Digital Repository of All Central and State Acts

question: What is the compensation scheme for women victims/survivors of sexual assault (NALSA Scheme)?
answer: Under Section 396 BNSS (formerly 357A CrPC) and the NALSA Compensation Scheme for Women Victims/Survivors of Sexual Assault, state governments must pay minimum compensation ranging from ₹4 Lakhs to ₹10 Lakhs for rape survivors, including interim medical compensation.
source_title: NALSA Official Portal

question: What is the Code on Wages, 2019 and what four legacy acts does it amalgamate?
answer: The Code on Wages, 2019 consolidates four central labour acts: 1. Payment of Wages Act, 1936, 2. Minimum Wages Act, 1948, 3. Payment of Bonus Act, 1965, and 4. Equal Remuneration Act, 1976, creating a universal statutory floor wage across all sectors.
source_title: India Code - Digital Repository of All Central and State Acts

question: What is the Floor Wage concept under Section 9 of the Code on Wages?
answer: Section 9 empowers the Central Government to fix a statutory Floor Wage taking into account minimum living standards of workers. State Governments cannot fix minimum wages below the Central floor wage.
source_title: India Code - Digital Repository of All Central and State Acts

question: What constitutes 'Wages' under the uniform definition across modern labour codes?
answer: Wages include basic pay, dearness allowance (DA), and retaining allowance. Specified exclusions (HRA, bonus, PF, overtime, gratuity) cannot exceed 50% of total remuneration; if they do, the excess is deemed wages for social security calculations.
source_title: India Code - Digital Repository of All Central and State Acts

question: When does Gratuity become payable under Section 4 of Payment of Gratuity Act, 1972?
answer: Under Section 4, gratuity is payable to an employee on termination of employment after rendering continuous service for not less than 5 years (waived in case of death or disablement) at the rate of 15 days' wages for every completed year of service, capped at ₹20 Lakhs.
source_title: India Code - Digital Repository of All Central and State Acts

question: Can an employer withhold or forfeit Gratuity of an employee?
answer: Under Section 4(6) of Payment of Gratuity Act, gratuity can be forfeited only to the extent of damage caused if the employee's services were terminated for riotous conduct, violence, or an offence involving moral turpitude during employment.
source_title: India Code - Digital Repository of All Central and State Acts

question: What are the eligibility criteria and contributions under the Employees' Provident Fund (EPF) Act?
answer: The EPF Act applies to establishments with 20 or more employees. For employees drawing basic wages up to ₹15,000/month (mandatory), employee and employer each contribute 12% of basic wages plus DA, with employer's share divided between EPF (3.67%) and EPS pension (8.33%).
source_title: EPFO Official Portal

question: What is Retrenchment under Section 2(oo) and 25F of the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947?
answer: Retrenchment is termination of a workman's service by employer for any reason other than disciplinary punishment, voluntary retirement, or superannuation. Under Section 25F, retrenchment requires 1 month notice (or pay in lieu) and compensation of 15 days' average pay per year of service.
source_title: India Code - Digital Repository of All Central and State Acts

question: What is the requirement of Government permission for Layoff and Retrenchment under Chapter V-B of IDA?
answer: Under Chapter V-B of IDA 1947, industrial establishments employing 100 or more workmen (raised to 300 in several state amendments and the Industrial Relations Code) must obtain prior permission from the appropriate Government before laying off, retrenching workmen, or closing down.
source_title: India Code - Digital Repository of All Central and State Acts

question: What is the definition of 'Workman' under Section 2(s) of the Industrial Disputes Act?
answer: Section 2(s) defines a workman as any person employed in an industry to do manual, unskilled, skilled, technical, operational, clerical, or supervisory work, but expressly excludes persons employed in a managerial or administrative capacity or supervisors earning above statutory wage caps.
source_title: India Code - Digital Repository of All Central and State Acts

question: What constitutes an Illegal Strike or Lock-out under Section 22 to 24 of IDA?
answer: A strike or lock-out in a public utility service is illegal if initiated without giving 6 weeks prior notice, or within 14 days of giving notice, or during pendency of conciliation proceedings before a Conciliation Officer or Labour Court.
source_title: India Code - Digital Repository of All Central and State Acts

question: What is the Payment of Bonus Act entitlement and wage threshold?
answer: The Payment of Bonus Act, 1965 applies to establishments with 20 or more employees. Employees drawing wages up to ₹21,000/month who have worked at least 30 days in an accounting year are entitled to a minimum bonus of 8.33% of wages (up to maximum 20%).
source_title: India Code - Digital Repository of All Central and State Acts

question: What is the Employees' State Insurance (ESI) Act coverage and benefits?
answer: The ESI Act, 1948 applies to non-seasonal factories and establishments employing 10 or more persons. Employees earning up to ₹21,000/month are covered for medical care, sickness benefit, maternity benefit, disablement benefit, and dependent benefits with 0.75% employee and 3.25% employer contributions.
source_title: ESIC Official Portal

question: What is Equal Remuneration under the Code on Wages, 2019?
answer: Section 3 of the Code on Wages prohibits discrimination on grounds of gender in matters relating to wages for the same work or work of similar nature, and prohibits gender-based discrimination in recruitment.
source_title: India Code - Digital Repository of All Central and State Acts

question: What are the rules regarding Maximum Working Hours and Overtime under Factories Act, 1948?
answer: Under Sections 51 and 54 of the Factories Act, 1948, no adult worker shall be required to work more than 48 hours in any week or more than 9 hours in any day. Under Section 59, overtime work beyond 9 hours/day or 48 hours/week must be paid at twice the ordinary rate of wages.
source_title: India Code - Digital Repository of All Central and State Acts

question: What is the Employee Compensation Act, 1923 (Workmen's Compensation)?
answer: The Employee's Compensation Act, 1923 mandates employers to pay compensation to employees or their dependents for personal injury, occupational disease, or death arising out of and in the course of employment.
source_title: India Code - Digital Repository of All Central and State Acts

question: Can an employer enforce a Non-Compete Clause against an employee in India?
answer: Under Section 27 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872, every agreement restraining anyone from exercising a lawful profession, trade, or business is void. Indian courts have consistently held post-employment non-compete clauses void and unenforceable as against public policy.
source_title: Supreme Court of India Official Portal

question: What are the legal rights of Contract Labour under the Contract Labour Act, 1970?
answer: Under the Contract Labour (Regulation and Abolition) Act, 1970, contract workers are entitled to basic amenities (drinking water, rest rooms, first aid), timely wage payment by 7th of each month, and if the contractor defaults, the principal employer is legally bound to pay wages.
source_title: India Code - Digital Repository of All Central and State Acts

question: What is the Social Security Code, 2020 recognition of Gig and Platform Workers?
answer: Section 114 of the Code on Social Security, 2020 introduces statutory recognition for gig workers and platform workers (e.g. ride-share drivers, delivery partners), establishing a Social Security Fund funded by aggregators contributing 1-2% of annual turnover.
source_title: India Code - Digital Repository of All Central and State Acts

question: What is the Occupational Safety, Health and Working Conditions Code, 2020?
answer: The OSH Code, 2020 consolidates 13 labour enactments concerning safety, health, and working conditions in factories, mines, docks, and construction sites, introducing statutory appointment letters for all employees and annual health checkups.
source_title: India Code - Digital Repository of All Central and State Acts

question: What are the rules regarding Notice Period and Termination Pay in Private Employment?
answer: Termination of private employment is governed by the employment contract and State Shops and Establishments Acts, which typically mandate 30 days written notice or pay in lieu, payment of accrued earned leave, and settlement of full and final dues within 2 working days.
source_title: India Code - Digital Repository of All Central and State Acts

question: Can pregnant women work night shifts in factories or commercial establishments?
answer: Under Section 43 of the OSH Code, 2020, women may be employed with their consent during night shifts (between 7 PM and 6 AM) subject to employer ensuring adequate safety, transportation, and conditions relating to holidays, working hours, and crèche facilities.
source_title: India Code - Digital Repository of All Central and State Acts

question: What is Fixed-Term Employment (FTE) under the Industrial Relations Code, 2020?
answer: The Industrial Relations Code, 2020 recognizes Fixed-Term Employment, allowing employers to hire workers for specific tenures directly. FTE workers are entitled to proportional statutory benefits (wages, leave, medical, gratuity on completing 1 year) equal to permanent workers.
source_title: India Code - Digital Repository of All Central and State Acts

question: What is the limitation period for raising an Industrial Dispute under IDA?
answer: Under Section 2A(3) of the Industrial Disputes Act, an application regarding discharge, dismissal, or retrenchment must be made to the Labour Court or Tribunal before the expiry of 3 years from the date of discharge.
source_title: India Code - Digital Repository of All Central and State Acts

question: What is Unfair Labour Practice under the Fifth Schedule of IDA?
answer: Under Section 25T and the Fifth Schedule of IDA 1947, employers and trade unions are prohibited from committing unfair labour practices—including victimizing workers for union activities, setting up employer-sponsored unions, or refusing collective bargaining.
source_title: India Code - Digital Repository of All Central and State Acts

question: What is the Samadhan Portal for online industrial dispute conciliation?
answer: The Ministry of Labour and Employment launched the Samadhan Portal (samadhan.labour.gov.in) enabling industrial workmen and unions to file dispute claims, conciliation applications, and track hearing dates electronically.
source_title: Labour Ministry Portal

question: What is the statutory interest penalty on delayed Gratuity payment?
answer: Under Section 7(3A) of Payment of Gratuity Act, if gratuity is not paid within 30 days from when it becomes payable, the employer is liable to pay simple interest from the expiry of the period at the rate notified by the Central Government.
source_title: India Code - Digital Repository of All Central and State Acts

question: What are the rules regarding deduction from wages under Code on Wages?
answer: Under Section 18 of Code on Wages, wage deductions are permissible only for specified reasons (fines, absence, damage to goods, house accommodation, advances, income tax, PF), and total deductions cannot exceed 50% of employee's total wages in any wage period.
source_title: India Code - Digital Repository of All Central and State Acts

question: What is the definition of 'Continuous Service' for gratuity computation?
answer: Under Section 2A of Payment of Gratuity Act, an employee is in continuous service for one year if they have actually worked under the employer for at least 190 days in a mine/seasonal establishment, or 240 days in any other establishment during 12 calendar months.
source_title: India Code - Digital Repository of All Central and State Acts

question: What are the rights of Inter-State Migrant Workers under OSH Code 2020?
answer: The OSH Code, 2020 entitles inter-state migrant workers to a journey allowance, toll-free grievance helplines, portability of ration and welfare benefits, and mandatory registration by contractors on the Shram Suvidha portal.
source_title: India Code - Digital Repository of All Central and State Acts

question: What is the e-Shram Portal for unorganised workers?
answer: The e-Shram portal created by the Ministry of Labour registers unorganised workers (construction workers, domestic staff, gig workers, street vendors) issuing a 12-digit Universal Account Number (UAN) for social security and insurance benefits.
source_title: e-Shram Portal

question: What are the essential elements of a valid contract under Section 10 of Indian Contract Act?
answer: Under Section 10 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872, all agreements are contracts if they are made by the free consent of parties competent to contract, for a lawful consideration and with a lawful object, and are not expressly declared to be void.
source_title: India Code - Digital Repository of All Central and State Acts

question: Who is competent to contract under Section 11 of the Indian Contract Act?
answer: Under Section 11, every person is competent to contract who is of the age of majority according to the law to which they are subject (age 18), who is of sound mind, and is not disqualified from contracting by any law to which they are subject.
source_title: India Code - Digital Repository of All Central and State Acts

question: What is the legal status of an agreement entered into by a Minor?
answer: In the landmark Mohori Bibee v. Dharmodas Ghose (1903) decision, the Privy Council held that an agreement entered into by a minor is void ab initio (void from inception) and cannot be enforced or ratified upon attaining majority.
source_title: Supreme Court of India Official Portal

question: What vitiates Free Consent under Section 14 of the Indian Contract Act?
answer: Consent is not free under Section 14 when it is caused by: 1. Coercion (Section 15), 2. Undue Influence (Section 16), 3. Fraud (Section 17), 4. Misrepresentation (Section 18), or 5. Mistake (Sections 20, 21, 22). Contracts caused by coercion, fraud, or misrepresentation are voidable.
source_title: India Code - Digital Repository of All Central and State Acts

question: What is Consideration and can a contract exist without consideration under Section 25?
answer: Consideration is something of value exchanged between parties. Under Section 25, an agreement made without consideration is void, except when in writing and registered on account of natural love and affection, a promise to compensate for past voluntary services, or a promise to pay a time-barred debt.
source_title: India Code - Digital Repository of All Central and State Acts

question: What is the Doctrine of Frustration of Contract under Section 56?
answer: Under Section 56 of the Contract Act, an agreement to do an act impossible in itself is void. A contract to do an act which, after the contract is made, becomes impossible or unlawful by reason of some supervening event (e.g. war, natural calamity) becomes void by frustration.
source_title: Supreme Court of India Official Portal

question: What is the difference between Liquidated Damages and Penalty under Section 74?
answer: Under Section 74, when a contract stipulates an amount payable on breach, the court will award reasonable compensation not exceeding the amount named, whether it is characterized as liquidated damages or penalty, without requiring strict proof of actual loss.
source_title: Supreme Court of India Official Portal

question: What compensation is recoverable for Breach of Contract under Section 73 (Hadley v. Baxendale rule)?
answer: Section 73 provides that the injured party is entitled to compensation for loss or damage which naturally arose in the usual course of things from the breach, or which parties knew to be likely to result. Remote and indirect loss or damage is not compensable.
source_title: India Code - Digital Repository of All Central and State Acts

question: What are Agreements in Restraint of Trade under Section 27?
answer: Under Section 27, every agreement by which anyone is restrained from exercising a lawful profession, trade, or business of any kind is void to that extent. The only statutory exception is the sale of the goodwill of a business within reasonable local limits.
source_title: India Code - Digital Repository of All Central and State Acts

question: What are Agreements in Restraint of Legal Proceedings under Section 28?
answer: Under Section 28, agreements restricting any party absolutely from enforcing their rights by usual legal proceedings or limiting limitation periods are void, except arbitration agreements referring present or future disputes to arbitration.
source_title: India Code - Digital Repository of All Central and State Acts

question: What is a Contingent Contract under Section 31 of the Indian Contract Act?
answer: Section 31 defines a contingent contract as a contract to do or not to do something, if some event, collateral to such contract, does or does not happen (e.g. contracts of insurance, indemnity, and guarantee).
source_title: India Code - Digital Repository of All Central and State Acts

question: What is a Contract of Indemnity vs Contract of Guarantee under Sections 124 & 126?
answer: Under Section 124, a Contract of Indemnity is a contract by which one party promises to save the other from loss caused by promisor's or third person's conduct (two parties). Under Section 126, a Contract of Guarantee is a tripartite contract to perform the promise or discharge the liability of a third person in case of default.
source_title: India Code - Digital Repository of All Central and State Acts

question: What is the liability of a Surety under Section 128 of the Contract Act?
answer: Under Section 128, the liability of the surety is co-extensive with that of the principal debtor, unless it is otherwise provided by the contract. The creditor can sue the surety directly without first exhausting remedies against the principal debtor.
source_title: Supreme Court of India Official Portal

question: What is Bailment and duties of a Bailee under Section 148 and 151?
answer: Bailment is the delivery of goods by one person to another for some purpose upon a contract that they shall be returned when purpose is accomplished. Under Section 151, the bailee is bound to take as much care of the goods as a person of ordinary prudence would of their own goods.
source_title: India Code - Digital Repository of All Central and State Acts

question: What is a Pledge and rights of Pawnee under Section 172 to 176 of Contract Act?
answer: A pledge is the bailment of goods as security for payment of a debt. Under Section 176, if the pawnor defaults in payment, the pawnee may bring a suit against the pawnor upon the debt or sell the pledged thing after giving reasonable notice of sale.
source_title: India Code - Digital Repository of All Central and State Acts

question: What is Agency and Ratification under Section 182 and 196 of the Contract Act?
answer: An Agent is a person employed to do any act for another (Principal) or represent another in dealings with third persons. Under Section 196, where acts are done by one person on behalf of another without knowledge or authority, the principal may elect to ratify or disown such acts.
source_title: India Code - Digital Repository of All Central and State Acts

question: What is Specific Performance of a Contract under the Specific Relief (Amendment) Act, 2018?
answer: Following the 2018 Amendment to Section 10 of the Specific Relief Act, 1963, specific performance of a contract is now mandatory for courts rather than discretionary, subject only to limited exceptions listed under Section 14 and 16.
source_title: India Code - Digital Repository of All Central and State Acts

question: What contracts cannot be specifically enforced under Section 14 of Specific Relief Act?
answer: Under Section 14 of SRA, contracts cannot be specifically enforced if: 1. A party has obtained substituted performance under Section 20, 2. The contract involves performance of a continuous duty which the court cannot supervise, 3. The contract is so personal in nature that court cannot enforce, or 4. The contract is determinable in its nature.
source_title: India Code - Digital Repository of All Central and State Acts

question: What is Substituted Performance under Section 20 of the Specific Relief Act?
answer: Under Section 20 of SRA, where a contract is broken, the party suffering breach has the option of substituted performance through a third party or agency and can recover expenses and costs incurred from the party committing breach after giving 30 days written notice.
source_title: India Code - Digital Repository of All Central and State Acts

question: What are the infrastructure project injunction bars under Section 20A of SRA?
answer: Section 20A of the Specific Relief Act prohibits courts from granting any injunction in suits relating to infrastructure projects specified in the Schedule (transport, energy, water, communication) where granting injunction would cause impediment or delay in project completion.
source_title: India Code - Digital Repository of All Central and State Acts

question: What is a Declaratory Decree under Section 34 of the Specific Relief Act?
answer: Under Section 34 of SRA, any person entitled to any legal character or to any right as to any property may institute a suit against any person denying it, and the court may make a declaration that they are so entitled without requiring further relief if none is seekable.
source_title: India Code - Digital Repository of All Central and State Acts

question: What is Novation, Rescission, and Alteration of Contract under Section 62?
answer: Under Section 62 of the Contract Act, if the parties to a contract agree to substitute a new contract for it (Novation), or to rescind or alter it, the original contract need not be performed.
source_title: India Code - Digital Repository of All Central and State Acts

question: What is Anticipatory Breach of Contract under Section 39?
answer: Under Section 39, when a party to a contract has refused to perform, or disabled themselves from performing, their promise in its entirety before the due date, the promisee may put an end to the contract unless they have signified acquiescence in its continuance.
source_title: India Code - Digital Repository of All Central and State Acts

question: What is a Quasi-Contract under Sections 68 to 72 of the Indian Contract Act?
answer: Quasi-contracts are legal obligations imposed by law in the absence of agreement to prevent unjust enrichment: 1. Necessaries supplied to incapable person (Sec 68), 2. Reimbursement for paying money on another's behalf (Sec 69), 3. Quantum meruit for non-gratuitous acts (Sec 70), 4. Finder of goods (Sec 71), and 5. Money paid by mistake or coercion (Sec 72).
source_title: India Code - Digital Repository of All Central and State Acts

question: What is Time as the Essence of Contract under Section 55?
answer: Under Section 55, when a party promises to do something at or before a specified time, and time is of the essence, failure to perform renders the contract voidable at the option of the promisee. In sale of immovable property, time is presumed not to be of the essence unless expressly stipulated.
source_title: Supreme Court of India Official Portal

question: What is Force Majeure clause in Indian commercial contracts?
answer: A Force Majeure clause excuses parties from contractual obligations upon the occurrence of unforeseen events beyond their control (pandemics, acts of God, war). In Energy Watchdog v. CERC (2017), the Supreme Court ruled that force majeure is governed by contract terms under Section 32, not general frustration under Section 56.
source_title: Supreme Court of India Official Portal

question: What is an Unconscionable Contract under Indian law?
answer: Under Section 16(3) of the Contract Act, where a person who is in a position to dominate the will of another enters into a transaction that appears on the face of it or on evidence to be unconscionable, the burden of proving that the contract was not induced by undue influence lies upon the person in dominance.
source_title: India Code - Digital Repository of All Central and State Acts

question: What is the limitation period for filing a suit for breach of contract?
answer: Under Article 55 of the Limitation Act, 1963, a suit for compensation for breach of any contract must be instituted within three years from the date when the contract is broken or when the breach ceases.
source_title: India Code - Digital Repository of All Central and State Acts

question: What is an Escrow Agreement in commercial transactions?
answer: An escrow agreement is a legal arrangement where an independent third party (escrow agent) holds assets, funds, or documents on behalf of transacting parties until agreed contractual conditions (e.g. regulatory approvals or delivery milestones) are satisfied.
source_title: India Code - Digital Repository of All Central and State Acts

question: What is the requirement of Stamping for commercial contracts in India?
answer: Under the Indian Stamp Act, 1899 and State Stamp Acts, commercial agreements must be stamped with prescribed stamp duty. Under Section 35 of the Stamp Act, an unstamped document cannot be admitted in evidence in court, but can be regularized on payment of deficit duty and penalty.
source_title: Supreme Court of India Official Portal

question: What is the SARFAESI Act, 2002 and how does it empower secured creditors?
answer: The Securitisation and Reconstruction of Financial Assets and Enforcement of Security Interest Act, 2002 empowers banks and financial institutions to enforce security interests and recover NPA loans by taking possession of mortgaged property without intervention of courts.
source_title: India Code - Digital Repository of All Central and State Acts

question: What is a 60-day Demand Notice under Section 13(2) of SARFAESI Act?
answer: Under Section 13(2), when a borrower defaults and the loan is classified as a Non-Performing Asset (NPA), the secured creditor issues a 60-day notice requiring the borrower to discharge liabilities in full, failing which the bank can take possession of secured assets.
source_title: India Code - Digital Repository of All Central and State Acts

question: What are the borrower's rights to object under Section 13(3A) of SARFAESI?
answer: Under Section 13(3A), the borrower may submit representations or objections within 60 days. The secured creditor must consider them and communicate reasons for non-acceptance within 15 days before taking possession.
source_title: India Code - Digital Repository of All Central and State Acts

question: What measures can a bank take under Section 13(4) of SARFAESI Act?
answer: If the borrower fails to pay, the bank may: 1. Take possession of secured assets, 2. Take over management of business, 3. Appoint a manager to manage secured assets, or 4. Require any debtor of the borrower to pay the bank directly.
source_title: India Code - Digital Repository of All Central and State Acts

question: What is the procedure for an appeal before the Debts Recovery Tribunal (DRT) under Section 17 of SARFAESI?
answer: Under Section 17 of SARFAESI, any aggrieved person (including borrower) can file a Securitisation Application (SA) before the DRT within 45 days from the date on which measures under Section 13(4) were taken by the bank.
source_title: India Code - Digital Repository of All Central and State Acts

question: What is the pre-deposit requirement for appealing from DRT to DRAT under Section 18 of SARFAESI?
answer: Under Section 18, an appeal to the Debts Recovery Appellate Tribunal (DRAT) requires the borrower to deposit 50% of the debt amount claimed by the creditor, which DRAT can reduce to not less than 25% for recorded reasons.
source_title: Supreme Court of India Official Portal

question: What is the Corporate Insolvency Resolution Process (CIRP) under Section 7 and 9 of IBC, 2016?
answer: Under the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016, a Financial Creditor (Section 7) or Operational Creditor (Section 9) can initiate CIRP against a corporate debtor before the National Company Law Tribunal (NCLT) for payment default exceeding ₹1 Crore.
source_title: IBBI Official Portal

question: What is the Moratorium under Section 14 of the IBC, 2016?
answer: Upon admitting an insolvency application, NCLT declares a statutory Moratorium prohibiting the institution or continuation of suits, execution of judgments, transfer of assets, or enforcement of security interests against the corporate debtor during CIRP.
source_title: IBBI Official Portal

question: What is the Committee of Creditors (CoC) under Section 21 of IBC?
answer: Section 21 mandates the constitution of a Committee of Creditors comprising all financial creditors of the corporate debtor. The CoC directs the resolution process, appoints Resolution Professionals, and votes on resolution plans (requiring 66% majority under Section 30(4)).
source_title: IBBI Official Portal

question: What is the strict 330-day timeline for CIRP under Section 12 of IBC?
answer: Under Section 12 of IBC 2016, CIRP must be completed within 180 days, extendable by 90 days. The overall maximum timeframe including litigation and legal extensions is 330 days, failing which the corporate debtor goes into liquidation.
source_title: IBBI Official Portal

question: What is the 'Waterfall Mechanism' for distribution of assets in liquidation under Section 53 of IBC?
answer: Section 53 establishes priority of asset distribution: 1. CIRP and liquidation costs, 2. Workmen's dues (24 months) and secured creditors pari passu, 3. Employee wages (12 months), 4. Unsecured financial creditors, 5. Government dues and remaining secured debts, 6. Operational debts, 7. Equity shareholders.
source_title: IBBI Official Portal

question: What is the RBI Integrated Ombudsman Scheme, 2021?
answer: The RBI Integrated Ombudsman Scheme integrates banking, NBFC, and digital payment ombudsmen into 'One Nation One Ombudsman' to resolve customer grievances against regulated entities free of charge, with compensation powers up to ₹20 Lakhs.
source_title: Reserve Bank of India Official Portal

question: What are the rules regarding unauthorized electronic banking transactions and customer liability?
answer: Under RBI Circular (July 2017), a customer has ZERO liability for unauthorized electronic transactions if caused by bank contributory fraud/negligence, or if customer reports third-party breach within 3 working days. Reporting within 4 to 7 days caps liability at ₹5,000 to ₹25,000.
source_title: Reserve Bank of India Official Portal

question: What are RBI Fair Practices Codes regarding loan recovery agents?
answer: RBI guidelines strictly prohibit recovery agents from resorting to intimidation, verbal/physical abuse, harassment, calling before 8 AM or after 7 PM, contacting debtor's relatives/friends without consent, or calling from unidentifiable phone numbers.
act_name: RBI Master Direction on Recovery Agents
source_title: Reserve Bank of India Official Portal

question: What is an Asset Reconstruction Company (ARC) under SARFAESI Act?
answer: An ARC registered with RBI under Section 3 of SARFAESI Act acquires non-performing loans from banks and financial institutions at discounted rates to unlock capital and restructure debts or realize secured assets.
source_title: India Code - Digital Repository of All Central and State Acts

question: What is CIBIL / Credit Information Bureau score and borrower rights?
answer: Credit Information Companies (Regulation) Act, 2005 (CICRA) regulates credit scoring agencies (CIBIL, Experian, Equifax). Borrowers have the statutory right under Section 21 to obtain one free credit report annually and dispute erroneous entries, which credit bureaus must resolve within 30 days.
source_title: CIBIL Official Portal

question: What is the Banking Regulation Act, 1949 and RBI's supervisory powers?
answer: The Banking Regulation Act, 1949 vests RBI with comprehensive statutory powers to license banks, inspect books, dictate lending policies, remove directors, and initiate restructuring or moratoriums (Section 45).
source_title: Reserve Bank of India Official Portal

question: What is the Recovery of Debts and Bankruptcy Act, 1993 (RDB Act)?
answer: The RDB Act establishes Debts Recovery Tribunals (DRT) and Appellate Tribunals (DRAT) for expeditious adjudication and recovery of debts due to banks and financial institutions where the debt amount is ₹20 Lakhs or more.
act_name: Recovery of Debts and Bankruptcy Act, 1993
source_title: India Code - Digital Repository of All Central and State Acts

question: What is an Original Application (OA) filed before DRT?
answer: An Original Application is a recovery suit filed by a bank before DRT under Section 19 of the RDB Act against defaulting borrowers and guarantors to obtain a Recovery Certificate enforceable by a Recovery Officer through attachment and sale.
source_title: India Code - Digital Repository of All Central and State Acts

question: Can agricultural land be attached under SARFAESI Act?
answer: Under Section 31(i) of the SARFAESI Act, the provisions of the Act DO NOT apply to any security interest created in agricultural land. Banks cannot take possession of or auction agricultural land under SARFAESI.
source_title: Supreme Court of India Official Portal

question: What is DICGC Deposit Insurance coverage limit for bank depositors?
answer: Under the Deposit Insurance and Credit Guarantee Corporation Act, 1961, bank deposits (savings, fixed, recurring) are insured up to ₹5 Lakhs per depositor across all branches of a failed or liquidated bank, with claims settled within 90 days.
source_title: DICGC Official Portal

question: What is the Banning of Unregulated Deposit Schemes Act, 2019 (BUDS)?
answer: BUDS Act 2019 bans all unregulated deposit schemes and chit frauds in India, penalizing running illegal deposit schemes with imprisonment up to 10 years and fines up to ₹50 Crores, and providing for attachment of property to refund depositors.
source_title: India Code - Digital Repository of All Central and State Acts

question: What are the legal regulations governing Digital Lending Apps in India?
answer: RBI's Guidelines on Digital Lending (2022) mandate that loan disbursals and repayments must execute directly between borrower's and bank's accounts without pass-through to third-party pool accounts, and prohibit lending apps from accessing mobile photos, contacts, and biometric data.
source_title: Reserve Bank of India Official Portal

question: What is the Pre-Packaged Insolvency Resolution Process (PPIRP) under IBC?
answer: Introduced via Chapter III-A of IBC 2016 for Micro, Small and Medium Enterprises (MSMEs) with default up to ₹1 Crore, PPIRP allows debtor-in-possession management to negotiate a pre-packaged resolution plan with creditors within an expedited 120-day timeframe.
source_title: IBBI Official Portal

question: What is the threshold default amount to initiate IBC against a company?
answer: Following Ministry of Corporate Affairs notification in March 2020, the minimum default threshold for initiating CIRP against a corporate debtor under Section 4 of IBC is ₹1 Crore (increased from ₹1 Lakh to protect MSMEs).
source_title: IBBI Official Portal

question: Can a homebuyer initiate insolvency against a real estate developer under IBC?
answer: Homebuyers are financial creditors under Section 5(8)(f) of IBC. However, under Section 7 proviso, an insolvency petition against a real estate promoter must be filed jointly by at least 100 allottees or not less than 10% of total allottees in the same project.
source_title: Supreme Court of India Official Portal

question: What is Section 29A of IBC (Disqualification of Resolution Applicants)?
answer: Section 29A disqualifies wilful defaulters, persons convicted of offences, undischarged insolvents, and promoters of NPA accounts for over one year from submitting a resolution plan, preventing errant promoters from buying back their stressed companies at a discount.
source_title: Supreme Court of India Official Portal

question: What is a Wilful Defaulter and its consequences under RBI guidelines?
answer: A borrower is classified as a wilful defaulter when they have the capacity to pay but intentionally default, or divert/siphon funds. Wilful defaulters are debarred from accessing banking facilities, floating new ventures, or serving as company directors.
act_name: RBI Master Circular on Wilful Defaulters
source_title: Reserve Bank of India Official Portal

question: What is National Financial Reporting Authority (NFRA) under Companies Act?
answer: Established under Section 132 of the Companies Act, 2013, NFRA is the independent regulator of auditing and accounting standards in India, empowered to investigate professional misconduct of auditors of listed companies and large public interest entities.
source_title: India Code - Digital Repository of All Central and State Acts

question: What is the procedure for an e-Auction of property under SARFAESI Act?
answer: Under Security Interest (Enforcement) Rules, 2002, the secured creditor must obtain a valuation report, fix reserve price, serve 30 days notice to the borrower, and publish a public e-auction notice in two leading newspapers, with bidder earnest money deposit (EMD) requirements.
source_title: India Code - Digital Repository of All Central and State Acts

question: What are the penalties for Drunken Driving under Section 185 of Motor Vehicles Act?
answer: Under Section 185 of the Motor Vehicles Act, driving with blood alcohol exceeding 30 mg per 100 ml of blood is punishable with imprisonment up to 6 months or fine up to ₹10,000 for the first offence, and imprisonment up to 2 years or fine up to ₹15,000 for a repeat offence within 3 years.
source_title: Ministry of Road Transport and Highways Official Portal

question: What is the Motor Accidents Claims Tribunal (MACT) under Section 165 of MV Act?
answer: Section 165 empowers State Governments to constitute Motor Accidents Claims Tribunals (MACT) to adjudicate claims for compensation arising out of motor accidents causing death, bodily injury, or damage to third-party property.
source_title: India Code - Digital Repository of All Central and State Acts

question: What is the Limitation Period for filing an accident compensation claim before MACT?
answer: Under Section 166(3) of the Motor Vehicles (Amendment) Act, 2019, an application for accident compensation before the Claims Tribunal MUST be filed within six months from the date of the occurrence of the accident.
source_title: Supreme Court of India Official Portal

question: What is Mandatory Third-Party Insurance under Section 146 of MV Act?
answer: Section 146 mandates that no motor vehicle can be driven in a public place without a valid third-party insurance policy covering liability for death, injury, or damage to property of third parties. Driving an uninsured vehicle attracts fine up to ₹2,000 or 3 months imprisonment (Section 196).
source_title: Ministry of Road Transport and Highways Official Portal

question: What is the Golden Hour and Good Samaritan protection under Section 134A of MV Act?
answer: Section 134A protects 'Good Samaritans' who render emergency medical or non-medical assistance to accident victims during the 'Golden Hour' from civil or criminal liability, police questioning, or compelled appearance as court witnesses.
source_title: Ministry of Road Transport and Highways Official Portal

question: What is the compensation for Hit and Run motor accidents under Section 161 of MV Act?
answer: Under Section 161 of MV Act (amended 2022 Scheme), the Central Government Compensation Scheme provides fixed compensation of ₹2,00,000 in case of death and ₹50,000 in case of grievous hurt to victims of hit-and-run motor accidents where the offending vehicle is untraceable.
source_title: Ministry of Road Transport and Highways Official Portal

question: What is the penalty for Driving without a valid Driving Licence under Section 181?
answer: Under Section 181 of the Motor Vehicles Act (as amended in 2019), driving without a valid driving licence is punishable with a fine of ₹5,000 or imprisonment up to 3 months, or both.
source_title: Ministry of Road Transport and Highways Official Portal

question: What are the legal liabilities of vehicle owners for offences committed by Juveniles under Section 199A?
answer: Section 199A holds the vehicle owner or parent strictly liable if a juvenile drives a motor vehicle: fine of ₹25,000 and imprisonment up to 3 years, vehicle registration canceled for 1 year, and the juvenile is barred from obtaining a driving licence until age 25.
source_title: Ministry of Road Transport and Highways Official Portal

question: What is the penalty for Over-Speeding under Section 183 of the Motor Vehicles Act?
answer: Under Section 183 of MV Act, driving at a speed exceeding the statutory maximum speed limit is punishable with a fine of ₹1,000 to ₹2,000 for Light Motor Vehicles (LMVs), and ₹2,000 to ₹4,000 for medium or heavy commercial vehicles.
source_title: Ministry of Road Transport and Highways Official Portal

question: What is the penalty for Dangerous / Reckless Driving under Section 184 of MV Act?
answer: Under Section 184, driving dangerously (including jumping red lights, using handheld mobile phones while driving, or driving against authorized flow of traffic) carries a fine between ₹1,000 and ₹5,000, or imprisonment up to 1 year, or both.
source_title: Ministry of Road Transport and Highways Official Portal

question: What are the rules regarding Seatbelts and Helmets under Sections 194B and 194D of MV Act?
answer: Under Section 194B, driving without wearing a safety belt attracts a fine of ₹1,000. Under Section 194D, riding a two-wheeler without wearing a protective BIS-compliant helmet attracts a fine of ₹1,000 and disqualification of driving licence for 3 months.
source_title: Ministry of Road Transport and Highways Official Portal

question: What is the penalty for Not Giving Way to Emergency Vehicles (Ambulance/Fire) under Section 194E?
answer: Under Section 194E of the Motor Vehicles Act, failure to draw to the side of the road and allow unobstructed passage to emergency vehicles (fire service vehicles or ambulances) is punishable with imprisonment up to 6 months or fine of ₹10,000, or both.
source_title: Ministry of Road Transport and Highways Official Portal

question: How is the Multiplier applied in calculating MACT death compensation (Sarla Verma case)?
answer: In Sarla Verma v. DTC (2009) and National Insurance Co. v. Pranay Sethi (2017), the Supreme Court standardized MACT compensation calculation based on: deceased's income, addition for future prospects, deduction for personal living expenses, and age-based multiplier (ranging from 18 for age 15-25 down to 5 for age over 65).
source_title: Supreme Court of India Official Portal

question: Can a traffic police officer seize a driving licence on the spot?
answer: Under Section 206 of the MV Act, an authorized police officer can seize a driving licence only if the driver is charged with specified offences: drunken driving, jumping red lights, over-speeding, using mobile phone while driving, or overloading passengers.
source_title: Ministry of Road Transport and Highways Official Portal

question: What is an e-Challan and how can a motorist verify or contest it?
answer: An e-Challan is an electronic traffic violation notice issued via automated speed cameras, CCTV, or handheld PoS machines. Citizens can verify, contest, or pay e-challans online through the official Parivahan portal (echallan.parivahan.gov.in) or Virtual Courts.
source_title: Parivahan Official Portal

question: What is the National Vehicle Scrappage Policy (2021)?
answer: Under the Voluntary Vehicle Fleet Modernization Program, private vehicles older than 20 years and commercial vehicles older than 15 years must undergo automated fitness tests. Vehicles failing automated fitness tests or not re-registered must be scrapped at Registered Vehicle Scrapping Facilities (RVSF).
source_title: Ministry of Road Transport and Highways Official Portal

question: What is a High Security Registration Plate (HSRP) and is it mandatory?
answer: Under Rule 50 of the Central Motor Vehicles Rules, 1989, all motor vehicles must display laser-branded tamper-evident High Security Registration Plates (HSRP) with a chromium-based hologram to prevent vehicle theft and cloning of number plates.
source_title: Ministry of Road Transport and Highways Official Portal

question: What is the Bharat Series (BH Series) vehicle registration?
answer: Introduced by MoRTH in 2021, BH series registration allows defense personnel, central/state government employees, and private sector employees with offices in 4 or more states to register vehicles seamlessly without requiring re-registration when moving across states.
source_title: Ministry of Road Transport and Highways Official Portal

question: What is the penalty for Overloading goods vehicles under Section 194 of MV Act?
answer: Under Section 194 of MV Act, driving a motor vehicle with weight exceeding permissible gross vehicle weight attracts a fine of ₹20,000 plus an additional ₹2,000 for each ton of excess load, alongside refusal of onward movement until excess load is offloaded.
source_title: Ministry of Road Transport and Highways Official Portal

question: What is the Pollution Under Control (PUC) Certificate requirement and penalty under Section 190(2)?
answer: Every motor vehicle must hold a valid computerized PUC Certificate. Under Section 190(2) of the MV Act, driving without a valid PUC attracts a fine up to ₹10,000 and/or imprisonment up to 3 months, alongside licence disqualification for 3 months.
source_title: Ministry of Road Transport and Highways Official Portal

question: What are the rules regarding driving licence validity for private light motor vehicles?
answer: Under Section 14 of the MV Act, a driving licence for a non-transport vehicle is valid for 20 years from issuance or until the holder attains the age of 40 years (whichever is earlier), followed by 10-year renewals up to age 50, and 5-year renewals thereafter.
source_title: Ministry of Road Transport and Highways Official Portal

question: What is the liability of an Insurance Company when the driver held a fake licence?
answer: In National Insurance Co. Ltd. v. Swaran Singh (2004), the Supreme Court ruled that the insurer must first pay the third-party victim and then recover the compensation amount from the vehicle owner ('pay and recover') unless the owner deliberately entrusted the vehicle knowing the licence was fake.
source_title: Supreme Court of India Official Portal

question: Can an accident victim claim compensation in two different forums (MACT and Workmen Compensation)?
answer: Under Section 167 of the Motor Vehicles Act, where death or bodily injury gives rise to a claim under both MV Act and Employee's Compensation Act, the claimant may claim compensation under either Act, but cannot claim under both.
source_title: India Code - Digital Repository of All Central and State Acts

question: What is the No-Fault Liability under Section 164 of the amended MV Act, 2019?
answer: Section 164 provides fixed compensation of ₹5,00,000 in case of death and ₹2,50,000 in case of grievous hurt arising out of motor accident without requiring the claimant to prove any wrongful act, neglect, or default of the vehicle owner or driver.
source_title: Ministry of Road Transport and Highways Official Portal

question: What are the rules regarding modifications to motor vehicles (exhausts, tint, bull bars)?
answer: Under Section 52 of MV Act and the Supreme Court ruling in Regional Transport Officer v. K.V. Nehru (2019), structural alterations, oversized tires, loud aftermarket exhausts, and dark sun control tint films violating VIS guidelines are strictly illegal.
source_title: Supreme Court of India Official Portal

question: What is the procedure for transfer of ownership of a motor vehicle under Section 50?
answer: Under Section 50 of MV Act, the seller must report ownership transfer within 14 days (within same state) or 45 days (if outside state) using Form 29 and 30, with a No Objection Certificate (NOC) under Section 48 from the registering authority.
source_title: Ministry of Road Transport and Highways Official Portal

question: What is the legal mandate regarding FASTag on National Highways?
answer: Under the National Highways Fee Rules, 2008 and MoRTH notifications, FASTag (RFID electronic toll collection) is mandatory on all motor vehicles. Entering a FASTag lane without a functional tag attracts double the toll fee.
act_name: National Highways Fee (Determination of Rates and Collection) Rules, 2008
source_title: NHAI Official Portal

question: What is the penalty for driving a motor vehicle without registration under Section 192?
answer: Under Section 192 of MV Act, driving an unregistered vehicle or a vehicle with expired registration is punishable with a fine up to ₹5,000 for first offence, and imprisonment up to 1 year or fine up to ₹10,000 for repeat offences.
source_title: Ministry of Road Transport and Highways Official Portal

question: What is the duty of a driver in case of an accident under Section 134 of MV Act?
answer: Under Section 134, the driver must secure medical attention for the injured person, report the accident to the nearest police station within 24 hours, and furnish insurance and registration particulars, unless unable to do so due to mob violence.
source_title: Ministry of Road Transport and Highways Official Portal

question: Can a traffic policeman take away vehicle keys from the ignition?
answer: Under police standing orders and Motor Vehicles rules, traffic police officers are not legally empowered to snatch or remove keys from vehicle ignition. Motorists can report harassment to traffic supervisory officers or vigilance helplines.
source_title: Ministry of Road Transport and Highways Official Portal

question: What is the Model Tenancy Act, 2021 and what are its key objectives?
answer: Approved by the Union Cabinet in 2021 for adoption by States, the Model Tenancy Act aims to balance rights of landlords and tenants, mandate written tenancy agreements, cap security deposits, establish Rent Authorities and Rent Courts, and eliminate civil court delays.
source_title: Ministry of Housing and Urban Affairs

question: What are the caps on Security Deposits under Section 11 of the Model Tenancy Act?
answer: Under Section 11 of MTA 2021, security deposits are capped at maximum two months' rent for residential premises, and maximum six months' rent for non-residential (commercial) premises, refundable upon vacating after deducting lawful arrears.
source_title: MOHUA Official Portal

question: Is a written and registered Tenancy Agreement mandatory under Section 4 of MTA?
answer: Under Section 4 of MTA 2021, all tenancies must be executed through a written agreement submitted jointly to the statutory Rent Authority within two months, which issues a unique tenancy registration number.
source_title: MOHUA Official Portal

question: Can a landlord cut off essential services (water/electricity) to force eviction?
answer: Under Section 20 of MTA 2021 and state rent control laws, landlords are strictly prohibited from withholding or cutting off essential services (water, electricity, elevator access) without just cause. Doing so attracts heavy penalties and rent authority directions to restore services immediately.
source_title: MOHUA Official Portal

question: What are the lawful grounds for Tenant Eviction under Section 21 of the Model Tenancy Act?
answer: Eviction is permitted only if: 1. Tenant fails to pay agreed rent for two consecutive months, 2. Tenant parts with possession/sublets without landlord's written consent, 3. Structural misuse or damage, 4. Bonafide requirement by landlord for self-residence after due notice.
source_title: MOHUA Official Portal

question: What compensation can a landlord claim if a tenant refuses to vacate after lease expiry?
answer: Under Section 23 of MTA 2021, if a tenant fails to vacate on lease expiry or termination notice, the landlord is entitled to double the monthly rent for the first two months of overstay, and four times the monthly rent thereafter until vacation.
source_title: MOHUA Official Portal

question: What is the requirement of prior notice before a landlord can enter rented premises?
answer: Under Section 15 of MTA 2021, a landlord or property manager must give at least 24 hours prior notice in writing (or electronically) before entering rented premises for inspection or repairs, and entry must occur between 7 AM and 8 PM.
source_title: MOHUA Official Portal

question: Who is responsible for repairs and maintenance under Section 15 and the Second Schedule of MTA?
answer: Structural repairs, whitewashing, plumbing, and electrical rewiring are the landlord's responsibility. Routine maintenance (replacing bulbs, tap washers, minor cleaning) is the tenant's responsibility. If landlord fails to repair, tenant can deduct cost up to 1 month's rent.
source_title: MOHUA Official Portal

question: What is the difference between a Lease and a Leave and Licence Agreement under Indian law?
answer: A Lease (Section 105 TPA) transfers an interest in immovable property with exclusive possession. A Leave and Licence (Section 52 Indian Easements Act) grants a personal permission to occupy premises without creating proprietary interest or tenancy rights, making vacation simpler upon expiry.
source_title: India Code - Digital Repository of All Central and State Acts

question: What is the mandatory 11-month rent agreement practice in India?
answer: Under Section 17(1)(d) of the Registration Act, 1908, leases of immovable property for any term exceeding one year (12 months or more) require compulsory registration. Parties often execute 11-month agreements to avoid mandatory registration and high stamp duty costs.
source_title: India Code - Digital Repository of All Central and State Acts

question: What are the statutory Rent Authorities and Rent Courts established under MTA?
answer: Sections 30 to 38 establish Rent Authorities (Deputy Collector level), Rent Courts (Additional Civil Judge level), and Rent Tribunals (District Judge level) with exclusive jurisdiction, barring civil courts from hearing tenancy disputes to achieve 60-day disposal.
source_title: MOHUA Official Portal

question: Can a landlord arbitrarily increase rent without notice?
answer: Under Section 8 and 9 of MTA 2021, rent can only be revised in accordance with the terms of the tenancy agreement, or by giving three months' prior written notice before revised rent becomes effective.
source_title: MOHUA Official Portal

question: What is Subletting and is it permissible without landlord consent?
answer: Under Section 7 of MTA 2021, no tenant can sublet whole or part of the premises, transfer, or assign rights without entering into a supplementary agreement with the landlord and informing the Rent Authority within one month.
source_title: MOHUA Official Portal

question: What happens to tenancy upon the death of the landlord or tenant?
answer: Under Section 5 of MTA 2021, tenancy agreement is binding on successors of both landlord and tenant. In case of tenant's death, rights of tenancy devolve upon their legal heirs for the remaining period of the tenancy agreement on the same terms.
source_title: MOHUA Official Portal

question: What is Statutory Tenancy under State Rent Control Acts?
answer: Under legacy State Rent Control Acts (e.g. Delhi Rent Control Act, Maharashtra Rent Control Act), a tenant whose contractual tenancy has expired is protected from arbitrary eviction as a 'statutory tenant' and can only be evicted on strictly proven statutory grounds.
source_title: Supreme Court of India Official Portal

question: What is Bonafide Need of the Landlord as an eviction ground?
answer: Under state rent control laws, a landlord can seek eviction if they genuinely and reasonably require the premises for their own residential or commercial occupation or for dependent family members, provided they do not possess other suitable alternative accommodation.
source_title: Supreme Court of India Official Portal

question: What notice period is required to terminate a monthly tenancy under Section 106 of TPA?
answer: Under Section 106 of Transfer of Property Act, 1882, in the absence of a written contract, a lease of immovable property for agricultural or manufacturing purposes requires six months' notice, and a lease for any other purpose (residential) requires 15 days' notice expiring with the end of a month of tenancy.
source_title: India Code - Digital Repository of All Central and State Acts

question: Can a tenant withhold rent if the landlord refuses to refund the security deposit?
answer: Tenants are not legally entitled to unilaterally adjust or withhold rent against security deposit unless explicitly permitted by the tenancy agreement. Proper remedy is to pay rent, vacate, and file for recovery of security deposit before the Rent Authority or Small Causes Court.
source_title: MOHUA Official Portal

question: What is a Rent Receipt and is a landlord legally bound to provide it?
answer: Under Section 10 of MTA 2021, every tenant who makes payment of rent or other charges is entitled to obtain a signed written or digital receipt immediately from the landlord acknowledging payment.
source_title: MOHUA Official Portal

question: What is the procedure for depositing rent before Rent Authority if landlord refuses to accept?
answer: Under Section 13 of MTA 2021, if the landlord refuses to accept rent or provide a receipt, the tenant may remit rent via bank transfer or deposit the rent with the Rent Authority within the prescribed period to avoid being held in default.
source_title: MOHUA Official Portal

question: What constitutes Material Impairment of property by a tenant?
answer: Making unauthorized structural alterations, knocking down load-bearing walls, or causing severe structural dampness that diminishes the utility or market value of the premises constitutes material impairment, giving landlord a statutory ground for eviction.
source_title: Supreme Court of India Official Portal

question: What are the rules regarding keeping pets in rented premises in India?
answer: The Animal Welfare Board of India (AWBI) guidelines and high court rulings stipulate that resident welfare associations (RWAs) or landlords cannot impose blanket bans on keeping pets. However, tenants must ensure pet hygiene and prevent public nuisance.
source_title: AWBI Official Portal

question: Can a commercial tenant claim rent waiver due to lockdowns or force majeure?
answer: In Ramanand v. Dr. Girme (Delhi High Court, 2020), the court held that temporary closure due to lockdown does not entitle a commercial tenant to automatic rent suspension unless there is a specific contract clause; tenants must pay rent or surrender tenancy under Section 108(B)(e) TPA.
source_title: Supreme Court of India Official Portal

question: What are the rules regarding Lock-in Periods in rental agreements?
answer: A lock-in period clause binds parties not to terminate the tenancy for a specified initial duration. If a tenant vacates during the lock-in period, the landlord can claim rent for the remainder only if genuine damages or lost opportunity are established under Section 73/74 Contract Act.
source_title: Supreme Court of India Official Portal

question: What is Mesne Profits payable by an unauthorized occupant after tenancy termination?
answer: Under Section 2(12) CPC, when a tenant continues in possession unlawfully after lease determination, they are liable to pay mesne profits calculated at current market rental rates, rather than old contractual rent.
source_title: Supreme Court of India Official Portal

question: What is the difference between Forfeiture of Lease and Determination by Efflux of Time?
answer: Under Section 111 of TPA, a lease determines automatically by 'efflux of time' when the agreed term expires. 'Forfeiture' occurs before expiry when the tenant breaches an express condition giving landlord a right of re-entry.
source_title: India Code - Digital Repository of All Central and State Acts

question: What is Relief Against Forfeiture for Non-Payment of Rent under Section 114 of TPA?
answer: Under Section 114 of TPA, where a lease is forfeited for non-payment of rent, the court may at the hearing relieve the tenant against forfeiture if the tenant pays or tenders all rent arrears with interest and costs within 15 days.
source_title: India Code - Digital Repository of All Central and State Acts

question: Can a tenant carry out commercial business in premises rented for residential purpose?
answer: Under Section 15 of MTA 2021 and municipal zoning laws, a tenant cannot use residential premises for commercial activities without landlord's consent and municipal sanction. Doing so constitutes unauthorized change of user justifying eviction.
source_title: Supreme Court of India Official Portal

question: What is the procedure for an appeal against an order of the Rent Court?
answer: Under Section 36 of MTA 2021, any person aggrieved by an order of the Rent Court may prefer an appeal to the Rent Tribunal (headed by a District Judge) within 30 days, which must endeavor to decide the appeal within 120 days.
source_title: MOHUA Official Portal

question: What protection do Senior Citizen landlords have for immediate possession under Rent Control laws?
answer: Several state rent control laws (e.g. Section 13A2 of Maharashtra Rent Control Act) provide summary proceedings allowing senior citizen landlords (age 65+) or retired defense personnel to obtain immediate possession of tenanted residential premises for self-residence.
source_title: Supreme Court of India Official Portal

question: What works are protected under the Copyright Act, 1957 in India?
answer: Under Section 13 of the Copyright Act, 1957, copyright subsists in original literary, dramatic, musical, and artistic works, cinematograph films, sound recordings, and computer programs/software source code.
source_title: Intellectual Property India Official Portal

question: What is the duration/term of Copyright protection in India?
answer: Under Section 22 of the Copyright Act, copyright in published literary, dramatic, musical, and artistic works lasts for the lifetime of the author plus 60 years counted from the beginning of the calendar year following the author's death (60 years from publication for films and sound recordings).
source_title: Intellectual Property India Official Portal

question: Is registration of Copyright mandatory in India?
answer: No. Copyright protection is automatic upon the creation and fixation of an original work in tangible form (Berne Convention). Registration under Section 44 and 45 of the Copyright Act is optional, though it serves as prima facie evidence of ownership in court.
source_title: Supreme Court of India Official Portal

question: What is Fair Dealing under Section 52 of the Copyright Act, 1957?
answer: Section 52 lists statutory exceptions where use of copyrighted work does not constitute infringement—including private or personal use, research, criticism, review, reporting of current events, judicial proceedings, and educational instruction.
source_title: Intellectual Property India Official Portal

question: What are the Moral Rights of an author under Section 57 of the Copyright Act?
answer: Section 57 grants authors perpetual moral rights independent of copyright ownership: 1. Paternity right (right to claim authorship), and 2. Integrity right (right to restrain or claim damages for any distortion, mutilation, or modification prejudicial to their honor or reputation).
source_title: Intellectual Property India Official Portal

question: What is a Trademark and what can be registered under the Trade Marks Act, 1999?
answer: Under Section 2(1)(zb) of the Trade Marks Act, 1999, a trademark is a mark capable of being represented graphically and distinguishing goods or services of one person from those of others, including brand names, logos, slogans, shapes of goods, packaging, or combinations of colors.
source_title: Intellectual Property India Official Portal

question: What is the difference between Trademark Infringement and Passing Off?
answer: Infringement (Section 29 TM Act) is a statutory remedy for unauthorized use of an identical or deceptively similar mark on registered goods. Passing Off (Section 27(2)) is a common law tort protecting unregistered marks against misrepresentation causing goodwill damage.
source_title: Supreme Court of India Official Portal

question: What is the validity period of a Trademark registration in India?
answer: Under Section 25 of the Trade Marks Act, 1999, trademark registration is valid for 10 years from the date of application and can be renewed indefinitely every 10 years upon payment of prescribed renewal fees.
source_title: Intellectual Property India Official Portal

question: What are Well-Known Trademarks under Section 11 of the Trade Marks Act?
answer: Under Section 2(1)(zg) and Section 11, a well-known trademark is recognized across India such that use of the mark on any goods or services (even completely unrelated categories) would indicate a connection, entitling it to cross-category protection.
source_title: Intellectual Property India Official Portal

question: What are the criteria for patentability under the Patents Act, 1970?
answer: Under Section 2(1)(j) of the Patents Act, 1970, an invention must satisfy three cumulative criteria: 1. Novelty (not published or used anywhere before), 2. Inventive Step (non-obvious to a person skilled in the art), and 3. Industrial Application (capable of being made or used in an industry).
source_title: Intellectual Property India Official Portal

question: What inventions are NOT patentable under Section 3 of the Patents Act?
